templates.title: Index efficiency: query shapes that examine far more documents than they return
templates.subtopic: conditional aggregation, ratio of sums, exact threshold comparison, deduplication

sections.scenario: A team running a document database wants to know which queries need a better index. For a day they set the database profiler to record every read on a replica set, and they loaded the profiler entries into a warehouse table. Public documentation describes the fields such an entry carries in general terms: the plan the query used (IXSCAN with an index, or COLLSCAN for a full collection scan), the number of index keys and documents examined, the number of documents returned, and a hash that identifies the query's shape (the same filter, sort and projection with different literal values). A query that examines thousands of documents to return a handful is the first one to fix. You have {{rows}} profiler rows.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over profiled_ops that returns ns, query_hash, executions, docs_examined, n_returned, examined_per_returned, collscan_executions: one row per query shape, identified by (ns, query_hash), that is inefficient. executions is the number of rows with op = 'query'; docs_examined and n_returned are the totals of those columns over the shape's rows. A shape is inefficient when it has at least {{min_execs}} executions and its total documents examined is strictly greater than {{k}} times its total documents returned. examined_per_returned is docs_examined / n_returned rounded to 2 decimal places, or NULL when the shape returned nothing. collscan_executions is the number of its executions whose plan_summary is 'COLLSCAN'. Order by ns, query_hash. {{getmore_rule}} {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The comparison with {{k}} is exact and strict: a shape that examined exactly {{k}} documents per document returned is not reported. The floor is inclusive. Compare totals, not rounded ratios.
sections.assumptions: The collections, query shapes, plans, counts and thresholds are hypothetical; profiling every operation is this exercise's setup (it adds load, and a real deployment would usually sample slow operations instead). The profiler field names are simplified; check current docs for the exact fields of a profiler entry.
sections.criteria: One row per (ns, query_hash); executions counted from query rows only; totals include the cursor's getMore batches (Hard+); ratio of totals, not an average of ratios; strict comparison with k done on exact integers and correct for zero returned; inclusive floor; COLLSCAN executions counted from query rows; duplicates removed by (host, op_id) and shapes kept apart by namespace (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss keys versus documents examined, sampling bias and how to verify an index change.

clarifications.q: Is the ratio the average of each query's ratio?
clarifications.a: No. It is the shape's total documents examined divided by its total documents returned. One query that returned a single document must not dominate.

clarifications.q: What about a shape that returned no documents at all?
clarifications.a: It still examined documents, so it is inefficient whenever it examined any; report it with a NULL ratio. Never divide by zero.

clarifications.q: Is the same query_hash in two collections the same shape?
clarifications.a: No. A shape is identified by (ns, query_hash).

clarifications.q: What is a getMore?
clarifications.a: A request for the next batch of an open cursor. It belongs to the query that opened the cursor: its work counts, but it is not another execution.

clarifications.q: Is the floor inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes: exactly {{min_execs}} executions qualifies.

clarifications.q: Does a getMore row of a collection-scan cursor count as a COLLSCAN execution?
clarifications.a: No. Only op = 'query' rows are executions.

hints: Aggregate once per (ns, query_hash): COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE op = 'query'), SUM(docs_examined), SUM(n_returned), and a filtered count for COLLSCAN.
docs > k × returned needs no division at all, and it works when returned is 0.
NULLIF(SUM(n_returned), 0) turns the zero denominator into NULL for the displayed ratio.
If rows can be delivered twice, deduplicate on the operation's identity before aggregating: DISTINCT ON (host, op_id).
followups: A shape returns 20 documents and examines 20 000 keys but only 25 documents. What does that tell you about the index, and which ratio would you add to the report?
The profiler at 100% costs too much in production. If you only had a sample of slow operations, which of these numbers would become biased, and how would you correct for it?
You recommend an index for the worst shape. How would you prove from the same data, a week later, that it helped and did not slow down writes?
The same report runs across thousands of clusters. How would you aggregate it so that one tenant's shapes are never shown to another, and so that the top offenders are still easy to find?

rules.ask: You averaged per-query ratios. Construct three executions where the average is above {{k}} and the ratio of totals is below it. Which one describes the cost?
A shape examined 5 000 documents and returned none. Is it reported, and how does your comparison treat it?
How do you attribute a getMore's work to the query that opened the cursor, and what would you do if a getMore row had no query row in the log?
Your HAVING clause holds two comparisons, the floor and the ratio. Which one is inclusive, which one is strict, and why compare totals rather than the rounded ratio?
Which columns identify one operation, and what would your deduplication do if two copies differed only in entry_id and logged_at?

templates.title: Time without a primary: seconds from losing a primary to the next election
templates.subtopic: per-member LAG, running counts over instants, as-of range joins, LATERAL lookups

sections.scenario: A replica set accepts writes only through its primary. When the primary steps down or becomes unreachable, the remaining members hold an election, and until a new primary is elected the set cannot take writes (public documentation describes this behaviour in general terms). A reliability team wants to know how long each of {{sets}} replica sets went without a primary, election by election, and to tell planned step-downs for maintenance apart from step-downs outside a window and from failures. A monitor recorded every member's state changes ({{changes}} rows); maintenance windows are in their own table.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns replica_set, lost_at, elected_at, new_primary, seconds_without_primary, cause: one row per gap. A replica set has a primary at an instant when at least one of its members' latest state at that instant is 'PRIMARY'. A gap starts at an instant when the set goes from having a primary to having none (lost_at) and ends at the first later instant when it has one again (elected_at); new_primary is the member that became 'PRIMARY' at that instant, and seconds_without_primary is elected_at − lost_at in seconds, with milliseconds. cause comes from the row at lost_at that took the primary out of that state: 'maintenance' when its reason is 'stepdown' and lost_at falls inside one of that set's maintenance windows [starts_at, ends_at), 'stepdown' for any other step-down, and 'failure' otherwise. Order by replica_set, lost_at. {{same_instant_rule}} {{repeat_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A member's state changes only through its own rows; every member has a 'snapshot' row at the start of the log. Order a member's rows by changed_at, change_id. A window's end is outside it.
sections.assumptions: Replica sets, members, timings and windows are hypothetical. The monitor's view stands in for the set's own view of itself, and its clocks are treated as exact; in a real set, members can briefly disagree about who is primary. Election timing depends on settings this exercise does not model; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Per-member previous state with a deterministic order; the number of primaries tracked per set, so a secondary's state change neither starts nor ends a gap; changes at one instant applied together (Hard+); a new primary elected before the old one steps down gives no gap (Hard+); the first later election ends the gap and names the member; seconds with milliseconds; cause from the reason and a half-open window (boundaries at Hard+); unchanged re-reports ignored and an open gap reported with NULLs (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss polling error, majority availability and month-level availability.

clarifications.q: A secondary goes into RECOVERING during a gap. Does that end the gap?
clarifications.a: No. Only a member becoming PRIMARY ends it.

clarifications.q: Can there be two primaries at once?
clarifications.a: In this log, briefly: a new primary can be elected before the old one is recorded stepping down. The set had a primary throughout, so there is no gap.

clarifications.q: Does a step-down during a maintenance window count as maintenance if it happens exactly at the window's end?
clarifications.a: No. Windows are [starts_at, ends_at).

clarifications.q: The primary becomes unreachable during a maintenance window. Is that maintenance?
clarifications.a: No. Only a step-down can be maintenance; an unreachable primary is a failure wherever it happens.

clarifications.q: Can the same member be elected again?
clarifications.a: Yes. new_primary is then the member that lost it.

clarifications.q: What is the unit of seconds_without_primary?
clarifications.a: Seconds, with the millisecond fraction, e.g. 4.217.

hints: Work out, for every row, the member's previous state with LAG(new_state) OVER (PARTITION BY replica_set, member ORDER BY changed_at, change_id). A row changes the number of primaries by +1, −1 or 0.
Sum those changes per (replica_set, changed_at), then take a running sum: the number of primaries after each instant. A gap starts where it falls to 0 and ends where it rises above 0.
For each gap start, the end is the first later instant with a primary: a LATERAL subquery with MIN, or LEAD over the starts and ends together.
The maintenance label is an EXISTS against the set's windows with a half-open range test.
followups: The monitor polls every 10 seconds instead of recording changes as they happen. What does that do to the measured gaps, and how would you report the uncertainty?
Writes using majority write concern can also stall when a majority of voting members is unavailable, even while a primary exists. How would you measure that kind of unavailability from similar data?
The team wants a monthly availability figure per replica set. How do you turn these gaps into one, and how should gaps that cross a month boundary or are still open be counted?
A driver retries a write across an election. What would you join to these gaps to measure what applications actually saw, rather than what the set reported?

rules.ask: You used LEAD over the rows. What does it return right after a gap opens when a secondary changes state before the election?
How do the row numbers help you find when the set had no primary, and what happens when two rows share a changed_at?
BETWEEN includes both ends. What does your query say about a step-down at exactly a window's ends_at?
The monitor repeats an unchanged PRIMARY state. How does your count stay correct when the same member reports PRIMARY twice?
Your gap is in seconds. How would you report availability over a month from it, and what do you do with a gap that is still open?

templates.title: Unused indexes: no recorded use on any replica-set member
templates.subtopic: counter deltas with resets, anti-joins, exclusion rules

sections.scenario: Every index speeds up some reads and slows down every write, and it takes memory and disk. A team wants to drop indexes nobody uses. Public documentation describes per-member index access statistics in general terms: each member of a replica set counts the operations that used each index since a point in time (usually when the member last started), and the count starts again from zero when the member restarts. The counts are per member, and reads sent to secondaries only show up on those secondaries. A collector sampled every member's counters once a day from {{window_start}} to {{window_end}} ({{n_samples}} samples, {{n_rows}} rows).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns cluster, ns, index_name, key_pattern, size_mb for every index that had no recorded use in the window, ordered by cluster, ns, index_name. For each member and index, compare each sample with the previous sample of the same member and index: if since is unchanged, the use in between is ops − previous ops; if since changed, the counter restarted after the previous sample and the use is ops. The first sample of each series is the baseline: what it counted happened before the window. An index was used in the window if any member shows use greater than 0 between any two consecutive samples. Exclude unique indexes (they enforce a constraint), TTL indexes (ttl_seconds is not NULL), and indexes built inside the window (created_at at or after {{window_start}}): they have not been observed for long enough. size_mb is size_bytes / 1048576 rounded to 1 decimal place. {{restart_rule}} {{cluster_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The window starts at {{window_start}}; you may write that timestamp into the query. Every index has a sample on every member at every sample time after it was built.
sections.assumptions: Clusters, collections, indexes, sizes and counters are hypothetical. The sampling schedule and the rules for what counts as use are this exercise's; check current docs for what increments an index's access counter and when it resets.
sections.criteria: Consecutive samples per member and index; use as an increase, with a restart (since changed) counted from zero (Hard+); the baseline sample not counted; use on any member, not just the primary; unique, TTL and built-in-window indexes excluded with an inclusive start (Hard+); indexes identified with their cluster (Very Hard); size rounded correctly; deterministic order; can discuss reversible drops, redundant indexes and collection at scale.

clarifications.q: An index's counter is 80 000 at the first sample and never changes. Is it used?
clarifications.a: No. That use happened before the window; only increases inside it count.

clarifications.q: The primary never used an index but a secondary did.
clarifications.a: It is used. Analytics reads routed to a secondary are real use, and dropping the index would hurt them.

clarifications.q: How do I recognise a restart?
clarifications.a: The sample's since differs from the previous sample's on that member.

clarifications.q: Is an index built exactly at the window's start inside the window?
clarifications.a: Yes: created_at >= {{window_start}} is inside, and it is excluded.

clarifications.q: What about the _id_ index?
clarifications.a: It is unique, so it is excluded with the other unique indexes.

hints: LAG(ops) and LAG(since) over PARTITION BY cluster, member, ns, index_name ORDER BY sampled_at give the previous sample.
Build the set of (cluster, ns, index_name) that were used on any member, then anti-join the index list against it with NOT EXISTS.
A CASE turns the two counter situations into one "use since the previous sample" value; the baseline row has no previous sample and is skipped.
followups: The team plans to drop the reported indexes next week. What would you do first to make the change reversible and to catch a monthly job that the window missed?
An index is used, but only by a query that another index would also serve. How would you find redundant indexes, not just unused ones?
Across thousands of clusters, the counters are collected every hour. How would you store them so that this report runs over any window cheaply, and how do you handle a sample that is missed?
An index is used rarely but each use is a critical, latency-sensitive read. How would you weigh the cost of keeping it against the cost of dropping it, with numbers you can collect?

rules.ask: Why is a primary's counter not enough to call an index unused, and which reads only ever reach a secondary?
A member restarted mid-window. What do max − min or last − first say about an index used only after the restart?
A counter is 80 000 at the first sample and never moves. Is that index in use during the window?
How would hiding the index before dropping it change your rollout, and what would you watch while it is hidden?

templates.title: TTL monitor passes: which documents each pass deletes
templates.subtopic: min-heap with lazy invalidation, event simulation

sections.scenario: A TTL index deletes documents automatically once a date field in them is older than the index's expireAfterSeconds. Public documentation describes the mechanism in general terms: a background task wakes up periodically and removes the documents that are due, so a document can outlive its expiry by up to one period, and applications that update or remove the date field change when, or whether, the document expires. A team is debugging "documents that disappeared too early" and "documents that never expired", and wants to replay a write log against this exercise's model of the passes to see exactly what each pass removed.
sections.problem: Implement ttl_passes(events, expire_after, period, n_passes, cap=None). events is a list of (t, op, doc_id, value) sorted by t (integer seconds). 'insert' creates the document with its TTL field set to value (an insert never reuses the id of a live document); 'update' sets the field of a live document to value; 'delete' removes a live document. An update or delete of a document that is not live (never inserted, deleted by the application, or already removed by a pass) does nothing. A document with a date v expires at v + expire_after. Passes run at times period, 2·period, …, n_passes·period; before the pass at time T, every event with t ≤ T has been applied, and the pass deletes every live document whose expiry is at or before T. {{value_rule}} {{cap_rule}} Return a list of n_passes lists: the doc_ids each pass deleted, ascending.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 events and about 5 000 passes, with tens of thousands of live documents at a time. Work per write should be O(log n); a pass must not look at documents that are not due.
sections.assumptions: The period, the expiry rule, the cap and the handling of non-date values are this exercise's model; check current docs for how a TTL index treats missing fields, non-date values, arrays and deletion batches. Clocks are exact and every pass finishes before the next event.
sections.criteria: Writes applied in order with t ≤ T before each pass; updates and deletes to non-live documents ignored; expiry at or before T is due; the field removed or set to a non-date stops expiry (Hard+); a heap with lazy invalidation, O(log n) per write; cap with earliest-expiry-first and doc_id ties, and arrays by their earliest date (Very Hard); results sorted per pass; can discuss heap growth, bulk expiry and replication of deletions.

clarifications.q: Is a document whose expiry equals the pass time deleted?
clarifications.a: Yes. Due means expiry ≤ T.

clarifications.q: An update arrives at exactly a pass time. Before or after the pass?
clarifications.a: Before: every event with t ≤ T is applied first.

clarifications.q: An update targets a document the previous pass removed.
clarifications.a: Nothing happens. It does not recreate the document.

clarifications.q: What does an update to None mean?
clarifications.a: The field is removed, so the document no longer expires, until a later update sets a date again.

clarifications.q: Can an id come back?
clarifications.a: Yes, an insert after the old document is gone creates a new document with that id.

hints: A min-heap of (expiry, doc_id) gives the next document due without scanning. Push a new entry on every insert or update that sets a date.

Do not search the heap when a document changes. Keep each live document's current expiry in a dict; when an entry is popped, it is valid only if the document is live and its current expiry equals the entry's.
Each pass pops while the smallest expiry is ≤ T; stale entries are discarded as they surface.
followups: Your heap keeps stale entries. How large can it grow, and when would you rebuild it?
A team bulk-loads 50 million documents with dates already in the past. What does the first pass do to the database, and how would you spread the deletions?
Product wants documents removed within one second of expiry instead of within a period. What does that cost, and what would you suggest instead for reads that must not see expired data?
Each replica-set member could run its own passes. Why does it matter that only one member decides deletions, and how do the other members learn about them?

rules.ask: You sort documents on every pass. How much work is that per pass with 50 000 live documents and 5 000 passes?
Removing an arbitrary entry from a binary heap is O(n). What does lazy invalidation do instead, and what does it cost in memory?
When is a popped entry stale, and does an id that is deleted and inserted again break your check?
How many documents does each pass touch in your design, and how does that grow with the number of live documents?

templates.title: Search postings: documents containing every query term, scored by term frequency
templates.subtopic: sorted posting-list intersection, top-k selection

sections.scenario: A full-text search index over a collection is, at its core, an inverted index: for every term, a posting list of the documents that contain it, sorted by document id, each with the term's frequency in that document. Public documentation of search products built on such indexes describes the idea in general terms; real scoring is far richer. A team is building a small matcher for an internal tool and wants the core right first: find the documents that contain every term of a query and rank them by a simple score, fast enough for hundreds of queries over hundreds of thousands of documents.
sections.problem: Implement search(postings, queries, k, deleted=None). postings maps each term to a list of (doc_id, tf) sorted by doc_id (each doc_id at most once per list, tf ≥ 1). For each query in queries (a list of terms), the matching documents are those that appear in the posting list of every required term. A document's score is the sum of its tf over the query's distinct required terms. Return one list per query: up to k pairs (doc_id, score), highest score first, ties by smaller doc_id. A required term with no posting list matches nothing, so its query returns an empty list. {{term_rule}} {{deleted_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 documents, about 1.3 million postings and 400 queries; a query's terms can have posting lists from a few dozen to 40 000 entries. The work for a query should depend on its own posting lists, not on the number of documents in the collection.
sections.assumptions: The vocabulary, frequencies, queries and deletions are hypothetical; the score is this exercise's, not the relevance scoring of any real search product. Terms are already normalised (lower case, no punctuation).
sections.criteria: Intersection that starts from the shortest required list and never scans the whole collection; correct score over distinct required terms; top k with the doc_id tie-break; absent terms handled; deleted documents filtered (Hard+); excluded terms and queries without a required term (Very Hard); a clear complexity argument in terms of posting-list lengths; can discuss galloping, phrase positions, deletes and distributed top k.

clarifications.q: What is returned for a query with fewer than k matches?
clarifications.a: All of its matches, in order. No padding.

clarifications.q: Can the same term appear twice in a query?
clarifications.a: Yes; it counts once, both for matching and for the score.

clarifications.q: Two documents have the same score.
clarifications.a: The smaller doc_id comes first.

clarifications.q: Are the posting lists sorted?
clarifications.a: Yes, by doc_id, and you may rely on it.

clarifications.q: Should I return the doc_ids of deleted documents?
clarifications.a: Never. Deleted documents can still sit in posting lists until the index is rewritten.

hints: Start from the shortest posting list among the required terms: no answer can be outside it.
For each further list, keep only the candidates that also appear in it: a two-pointer merge over the sorted lists, or a binary search per candidate when the other list is much longer.
Pick the top k with heapq.nsmallest(k, ..., key=lambda e: (-score, doc_id)) or a sort of the (usually short) survivors.
followups: One query term appears in 40 000 documents and another in 30. Compare a linear merge with binary searches (or galloping) for this pair, and say when each wins.
The index must also support phrase queries ("replica set" as adjacent words). What would you add to each posting, and how does the intersection change?
Deleted documents pile up in posting lists. When would you rewrite the lists, and what does deletion cost a query in the meantime?
The collection is split across shards, each with its own index. How do you compute a global top k, and what must each shard return so the result is exact?

rules.ask: Building a set from each posting list costs the full list on every query. When is that fine, and when does the shortest-first approach win?
How does your query cost grow with the number of documents in the collection, and what does that mean at 300 000 documents and 400 queries?
Binary searching each candidate in a long list costs O(m log n). When does a linear merge beat it?
You sort all matches to take the top k. What does that cost when a query matches 40 000 documents, and what would you use instead?

templates.title: Routing change events to thousands of change-stream subscriptions
templates.subtopic: match counting over equality filters, null and $in semantics

sections.scenario: An application built on a document database pushes live updates to its users: a customer's order page refreshes when that order changes, a warehouse screen shows new deletes in one collection, a support tool follows one SKU. Opening one change stream per screen would mean thousands of streams on the cluster, so one service reads a single change stream and fans each change event out to many lightweight subscriptions. Each subscription is a filter of equality clauses on fields of the event. The fan-out step must decide, for every event, which subscriptions it matches, fast enough to keep up with the stream.
sections.problem: Implement match_subscriptions(subscriptions, events). subscriptions is a list of (sub_id, filter) with distinct integer ids. A filter is a dict that maps a field path (for example 'fullDocument.status') to a clause. An event is a flat dict from field path to value; fields can be missing, for example a delete event has no fullDocument fields. A subscription matches an event when every clause of its filter holds. An empty filter matches every event. A plain clause value holds when the event has that field and its value equals the clause value; values are strings and integers, and the integer 7 is not the string '7'. {{in_rule}} {{null_rule}} Return a list with one entry per event, in event order: the ids of the matching subscriptions in ascending order (an empty list if none match).
sections.constraints: Up to 20 000 subscriptions and 3 000 events in the timing check, each subscription with up to three clauses. Most clauses name a selective field such as a customer or a document id. Testing every subscription against every event is too slow; aim to touch only the subscriptions that share at least one field value with the event.
sections.assumptions: Event fields, filters and volumes are hypothetical, and events are already flattened to dotted field paths. Values are scalars (no arrays, no nested documents, no booleans or floats). Subscriptions do not change while a batch of events is matched.
sections.criteria: Correct matches in ascending id order; every clause required, not one; strict value types (7 is not '7'); empty filters match everything; $in with duplicates and empty lists handled; None matching missing and null fields where the rules say so; an inverted index on (field, value) with per-event hit counting, or an equally selective scheme; a clear complexity argument in terms of postings touched, not subscriptions; credible answers on skewed clauses, live updates and resuming the stream.

clarifications.q: Does the order of subscriptions in the input matter?
clarifications.a: No. Each event's list is sorted by subscription id.

clarifications.q: Is a clause on a field the event does not have false?
clarifications.a: Yes for a plain value, and for $in unless the rules for None below say otherwise.

clarifications.q: Can one filter name the same field twice?
clarifications.a: No. A filter is a dict, so each field appears at most once.

clarifications.q: What does a subscription with an empty filter match?
clarifications.a: Every event, including deletes.

clarifications.q: Do I need to handle range operators like $gt?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. The follow-ups ask what would change if you did.

hints: Turn the question around: instead of asking each subscription about the event, ask the event which subscriptions have a clause on each of its (field, value) pairs.
A subscription matches when the number of its clauses that hold equals the number of clauses it has. Count hits per subscription for the current event.
Subscriptions with no clauses never get a hit, and clauses satisfied by a missing field have no (field, value) pair in the event. Both need their own small list.
followups: Most subscriptions add operationType or the collection name as a clause. What happens to your hit counting, and how would you choose which clause to index a subscription under?
Subscriptions are added and removed thousands of times a minute. How do you update your index without rebuilding it, and what does an event see while a subscription is half-added?
A product team wants range clauses, such as fullDocument.total > 100. How would you index those alongside the equality clauses?
The fan-out service restarts. How does it resume the change stream without losing or repeating events for subscribers, and what happens if it was down longer than the oplog window?

rules.ask: How many filter checks is that for 20 000 subscriptions and 3 000 events, and how long would CPython take?
You intersect the sets of subscriptions per clause. What does that cost when one clause is operationType = 'update', shared by half of all subscriptions?
A subscription lists the same value twice in $in. Can your count go above its number of clauses, and what would it then return?
An event has no fullDocument.status field at all. Which subscriptions does it match, and how does your index find them without a (field, value) pair?
The stream resumes from a token after a restart. Which events might a subscriber see twice, and how would the service tell?

templates.title: Orphaned documents left behind by chunk migrations
templates.subtopic: range lookup over a routing table, replaying a migration log

sections.scenario: A sharded document database splits a collection's shard-key space into contiguous ranges called chunks, and each chunk is owned by one shard. A balancer moves chunks between shards to even out data. A migration copies the documents to the recipient shard, commits the new owner, and the donor deletes its copies later. If a migration aborts, or the donor's cleanup has not run yet, documents are left on a shard that does not own their range: orphaned documents. Queries routed through the router skip them, but a backup check, a count run directly on a shard, or a capacity report reads them. An operator wants an exact list of orphans per shard before running a cleanup.
sections.problem: Implement find_orphans(chunks, documents, migrations=None). chunks is a list of (min_key, max_key, shard) ranges, not sorted, that together cover every key exactly once. A range includes min_key and excludes max_key; None as min_key is the lowest possible key and None as max_key the highest. documents lists every document stored on every shard as (shard, doc_id, shard_key); the same doc_id can appear on two shards when a copy was left behind. {{migration_rule}} {{key_rule}} A document is orphaned when the shard that stores it is not the owner of the chunk that contains its key. Return the orphaned documents as (shard, doc_id) tuples sorted by shard and then by doc_id, or an empty list if there are none.
sections.constraints: Up to 20 000 chunks, 200 000 documents and 5 000 migrations in the timing check. Checking every chunk for every document is too slow, and so is scanning the chunk list for every migration. Aim for O((c + n) log c) or better for c chunks and n documents.
sections.assumptions: The routing table, shard names, keys and migration log are hypothetical. Every migration names a chunk that exists. A shard may own no chunk at all, for example one that is being removed. Chunk merges and splits are out of scope for this exercise.
sections.criteria: Correct orphans with the inclusive lower bound and exclusive upper bound; the lowest and highest chunks handled without comparing with None; copies on two shards reported only for the non-owner; a shard with no chunks treated as holding only orphans; committed migrations applied in order and aborted ones ignored; compound keys compared field by field; sorted bounds and binary search, or a sorted merge, with a correct complexity argument; credible answers on scale, concurrent migrations and range cleanup.

clarifications.q: Which chunk owns a key equal to a chunk boundary?
clarifications.a: The chunk whose min_key equals it. Ranges include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound.

clarifications.q: Are the chunks sorted?
clarifications.a: No. They come in no particular order.

clarifications.q: If a document is on its owner and also on another shard, what do I return?
clarifications.a: Only the copy on the shard that does not own the chunk.

clarifications.q: How do I compare None with a key?
clarifications.a: As a min_key it is below every key, and as a max_key above every key. Python cannot compare None with a number, so handle it yourself.

clarifications.q: Does an aborted migration change anything?
clarifications.a: Not the owner. It is often how orphans appear, because documents were copied before the abort.

hints: Every chunk is named by its lower bound, and the bounds never change. A dict from lower bound to owner lets you apply each migration in constant time.
Sort the lower bounds once. The chunk that contains a key is the one with the largest lower bound that is at most the key: one binary search.
Keep the lowest chunk (min_key None) out of the sorted list, and use it when the binary search finds no bound at or below the key.
followups: The cluster has 300 million documents across many shards. How would you find orphans without pulling every document's key to one machine?
A migration commits while your scan is running. Which documents could your report get wrong, and how would you make the scan safe?
Cleanup deletes orphans by range. Why delete whole ranges rather than individual documents, and what must be true before a range on the donor can be deleted?
Chunks are also split and merged during the window. What changes in your replay, and what identifies a chunk now?

rules.ask: How many comparisons is that for 200 000 documents and 20 000 chunks?
A key equals a chunk's lower bound. Which side does your search land on, and which bisect function gives that?
Sorting the documents first works. What does it cost compared with a binary search per document, and which would you use when documents arrive as a stream?
How does your code compare a key with the lowest and highest bounds without comparing an integer with None?
Two keys share the region and differ in the number. Show which chunk each one lands in, and what a chunk boundary with only the region set would mean.

templates.title: Debug the slow-query shape normaliser
templates.subtopic: recursive normalisation, canonical keys, units, malformed input

sections.scenario: A database team collects slow-query log entries from their clusters and groups them by query shape: the filter with every literal value replaced, so that {status: "paid"} and {status: "shipped"} count as one shape. The report ranks shapes by total time and drives which indexes get built. People have started to distrust it. Fast queries sometimes appear as the slowest in the report. The same query shows up as several shapes depending on how many values its $in list had, or on the order a driver wrote its range operators. Case-insensitive name searches are a different shape from case-sensitive ones. And a few shapes with oddly short filters appear that nobody can find in the application code. The normaliser below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix summarise_shapes(lines) so that it meets this specification. lines is a list of log lines as strings. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Skipped lines. A line that is not valid JSON (the log shipper cut it off) is skipped and counted in skipped. A line that parses but has a "truncated" key is also skipped and counted: in this exercise the server marks entries whose filter it shortened that way, so their shape cannot be trusted.
  2. Entries. Every other line is an object with "ns" (the namespace), "filter" (a dict) and "dur" (a duration string: an integer followed by us, ms or s). Other keys are ignored. Durations are converted to integer microseconds.
  3. Shape. Normalise the filter recursively. In a dict, every key is kept and its value normalised, except that in a dict containing "$regex" the "$options" key is dropped (options belong to the regex literal). The value of "$and", "$or" or "$nor" is a list of filters: normalise each one and keep their order. Any other list, such as the argument of $in or $nin, is one literal and becomes "?" whatever its length. Every other value becomes "?".
  4. Canonical form. The shape is json.dumps(normalised, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")), so keys are sorted at every level.
  5. Output. Group by (ns, shape). Return {"shapes": [{"ns", "shape", "count", "total_us", "max_us"}, ...], "skipped": n}, with shapes sorted by total_us descending, then ns, then shape.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 60 000 lines in the timing check, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: The log format and its "truncated" marker are this exercise's simplification of structured database logs; check current docs for the real format. Filters contain only ASCII field names, operators and values. Durations are always one of the three units.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom in the report; durations converted with the longer suffixes checked first; non-logical lists collapsed to one literal; keys sorted at every level; $options dropped beside $regex; entries marked truncated skipped and counted; the fix stays minimal and linear; adds a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Is {"$in": ["a"]} the same shape as {"$in": ["a", "b", "c"]}?
clarifications.a: Yes. The whole list is one literal.

clarifications.q: Are $or branches in a different order the same shape?
clarifications.a: No. Branches are kept in order; only keys are sorted.

clarifications.q: Does $options matter when there is no $regex beside it?
clarifications.a: That does not occur in this log. The rule applies to a dict that has $regex.

clarifications.q: Are skipped lines part of any shape?
clarifications.a: No. They only add to skipped.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Convert 850us, 120ms and 2s by hand, then trace each one through the duration helper.
Normalise {"status": {"$in": ["a", "b"]}} and {"status": {"$in": ["a", "b", "c"]}} with the current code and compare the strings.
Write the canonical string for {"total": {"$lt": 9, "$gte": 1}}. Which level of the dict gets sorted?
Read rule 1 again, then look for the place in the code that applies it.
followups: The report now merges shapes correctly, but two different queries with the same shape need different indexes because one sorts. What would you add to the shape key, and what would you leave out?
A filter compares a field with a date, written in the log as a typed literal object. What does your normaliser do with it, and what should it do?
Truncated entries are 3% of lines but 40% of the time spent. What would you report about them instead of dropping them silently?
Logs from 10 000 clusters arrive continuously. How would you compute the same report incrementally, and how would you keep a shape's identity stable when the normaliser's rules change?

rules.ask: Sorting keys merges {a, b} with {b, a}. Should it also sort $or branches, and what would that do to shapes that differ only in branch order?
Your parser for durations uses a regular expression. What does it do with 1.5s or 120 ms, and what should the report do with such a line?
Which exceptions do you catch, and around which statements? What would a broad except hide in this function?
Where could a fractional microsecond appear, and how do you keep the totals exact?
You store a hash of the shape instead of the string. How would someone reading the report find the query behind it?

templates.title: Heavy analytics on dedicated read members of an operational cluster
templates.subtopic: analytics members, read preference, replication lag, materialised summaries

sections.scenario: An online retailer runs its orders, carts and inventory on a document database cluster that holds about {{data_size}} and serves {{ops_rate}} at peak. The business wants dashboards and ad hoc aggregations over {{report_window}}: revenue by region and hour, conversion from cart to order, stock-outs by warehouse. Results must be no more than {{freshness}} behind the application. Last quarter an analyst's aggregation ran on the primary during a sale, scanned most of the orders collection, and doubled checkout latency for twenty minutes.
sections.problem: Design how analytics runs against this operational data without hurting the primary workload. Cover where analytical reads run (dedicated read-only members, a separate copy, or both), how clients are routed to them, what replication lag means for freshness and how you measure it, which indexes and pre-aggregated summaries you need and where they are written, how you stop a single heavy query from hurting either the application or other analysts, and what happens to dashboards when a member fails or an election happens.
sections.constraints: Checkout latency must not change when analytics runs. Analytics members must never become primary. Results must be at most {{freshness}} stale, and a dashboard must say when it is not. The data stays in one cluster unless you justify a copy elsewhere.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, freshness targets and the retailer are hypothetical. The cluster is a replica set (or a sharded cluster whose shards are replica sets). Read preference with tag sets, priority-0 non-voting members and a maximum-staleness setting exist as general product features; their exact behaviour is this exercise's rule, so check current docs.
sections.criteria: Analytical reads isolated on priority-0 (and justified voting or non-voting) members reached by tagged read preference; no fallback that silently sends heavy reads to the primary or the electable secondaries; freshness measured from replication lag and shown on dashboards; awareness that indexes and $merge/$out writes reach the primary; pre-aggregated summaries with a defined grain and update path; per-query limits (time limits, concurrency caps, a separate pool for ad hoc work); behaviour under member failure and elections; a reasoned threshold for moving analytics to a separate store.

clarifications.q: Can I build indexes only on the analytics members?
clarifications.a: In this exercise's rules, an index build replicates to every data-bearing member of the replica set, so an index you add for analytics also costs writes and memory on the primary. Check current docs.

clarifications.q: Where do the writes of an aggregation that ends in $merge or $out go?
clarifications.a: To the primary, even when the pipeline reads from a secondary, under this exercise's rules. Check current docs.

clarifications.q: Are the analytics members voting members?
clarifications.a: You decide, and you must say what it does to elections and to majority writes.

clarifications.q: Do analysts write arbitrary pipelines, or only use dashboards?
clarifications.a: Both: fixed dashboards for most people, and ad hoc pipelines for a dozen analysts.

hints: Separate the two questions: where analytical reads run, and where analytical results are stored. They have different costs on the primary.
Replication lag is a measurement, not a setting. Decide how a dashboard learns how stale its data is.
List what the analytics members still share with the primary: the replication stream, the index set, and anything written back.
followups: An analyst needs an index the application never uses. What does it cost on the primary, and what would you do instead?
The analytics member falls 20 minutes behind during a bulk import. What do the dashboards show, and what do the routing rules do?
Dashboards over {{report_window}} still scan too much. Design the pre-aggregated summaries: grain, how they are updated, and where they live.
Leadership wants to join this data with marketing data from another system. When does a copy into an analytical store become the better design, and how do you keep it fresh?
With {{ops_rate}} at peak, which numbers would you watch to prove analytics is not hurting checkout?

rules.ask: Drivers do not route reads to a hidden member in this exercise's rules. How do your dashboards reach it, and what does a hidden member cost you?
Your read preference allows any secondary. What happens to the electable secondaries, and to failover capacity, when a heavy aggregation lands on one of them?
The pipeline reads from an analytics member, but where do its writes go, and what does that add to the primary and the oplog?
Indexes replicate to every member. What does an analytics-only index cost the primary in write work and cache?
Your copy is fed from a change stream. What happens if the consumer is down longer than the oplog window, and how do you rebuild?
If every analytics member is staler than your limit, where do the reads go, and is that what you want during a sale?

templates.title: Index suggestion analytics across many clusters
templates.subtopic: query-shape aggregation, recommendation lifecycle, measuring impact

sections.scenario: A cloud database service offers a performance advisor: it looks at the slow operations on a customer's cluster and suggests indexes that would help. The product team wants an analytics pipeline behind that feature across {{clusters}} customer clusters, which report about {{shape_events}} slow-operation records a day, grouped into query shapes with literal values removed. Suggestions are computed from the last {{lookback}}. About {{accept_rate}} of suggestions are accepted. The team wants to know which suggestions are worth showing, and whether an accepted one actually helped.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from slow-operation records to suggestions and their measured outcome. Cover what is collected per cluster and what is never collected, how records are aggregated by cluster, namespace and shape, how candidate indexes are derived and compared with existing indexes, how suggestions are stored with a lifecycle (shown, dismissed, accepted, built, dropped), how you measure the effect of an accepted suggestion on its shapes and on the cluster's writes, and the reports the product team and a customer see.
sections.constraints: Literal values from customer queries must never be stored. Each customer sees only their own clusters. A suggestion must not be shown again after it was dismissed unless the workload changed materially. "Helped" must be measured, not assumed, and must account for workload changes between the before and after periods.
sections.assumptions: Cluster counts, volumes, acceptance rates and the record format are hypothetical. Each record carries a cluster, a namespace, a query shape, a plan summary, keys examined, documents examined, documents returned, a duration and whether the query sorted in memory. Index build and drop events are available from the cluster's metadata. Guidance such as ordering index fields by equality, then sort, then range is a public rule of thumb; treat it as this exercise's rule.
sections.criteria: Shape-only collection with literals excluded by design and tested; hourly aggregates by cluster, namespace and shape; candidate indexes derived with a stated rule and checked against existing indexes by prefix; suggestions as entities with a lifecycle and dismissal memory; acceptance learned from index metadata; impact measured per execution with a before/after window and a control, including write cost; tenant isolation; a credible scaling plan.

clarifications.q: Do we see the actual filter values?
clarifications.a: No. Shapes only, with literals replaced; the pipeline must keep it that way.

clarifications.q: Who builds the index?
clarifications.a: The customer, from the suggestion or on their own. You learn about it from the index metadata, not from the click.

clarifications.q: What counts as an existing index covering a suggestion?
clarifications.a: You define it. For example, an existing index whose leading fields equal the suggestion's fields in order.

clarifications.q: Is a suggestion per shape or per collection?
clarifications.a: You decide. Several shapes on one collection may be served by one index.

clarifications.q: How soon after a build can we judge it?
clarifications.a: Builds take time and workloads are weekly, so state the window you would use and why.

hints: Aggregate by (cluster, namespace, shape) per hour first; almost every later question is a join against that table.
Treat a suggestion as an entity with a stable id and a history of states, not as a row that is recomputed every day.
For impact, compare the same shapes before and after the build, normalised per execution, and use shapes the index cannot affect as a control.
followups: Two suggestions on one collection overlap: one on {status, createdAt}, one on {status}. How do you deduplicate, and what does the customer see?
Accepted suggestions show lower latency, but the customer also upgraded their cluster tier that week. How do you separate the effects?
An accepted index slowed writes on a hot collection. Where does that show up in your data, and how does it change what you suggest next time?
At {{shape_events}} records a day from {{clusters}} clusters, which stage is your bottleneck, and what would you pre-aggregate on the cluster side?

rules.ask: Where in your pipeline could a literal value slip through, for example inside a regex or an $in list, and how would you test that it never does?
Latency fell after the build, but so did the query volume. Which per-execution measure would you use instead, and why?
You cannot randomly build indexes on customers' clusters. What comparison would you use instead, and what bias does it carry?
How do you decide that the workload changed enough to show a dismissed suggestion again?
A suggested index was built and then never used. What does your report say, and what would you suggest to the customer?

templates.title: A product catalogue as documents — embed or reference, variants, attributes and arrays that never stop growing
templates.subtopic: embed versus reference, attribute pattern, bounded arrays, multikey indexes

sections.scenario: An online retailer is moving its catalogue of about {{products}} products into a document database. A product has a title, brand, category path, images and descriptions in several languages, and variants (size, colour, material), each with its own SKU, price and stock; the largest products have up to {{max_variants}} variants. Categories carry very different attributes (a laptop has screen size and RAM, a shoe has width and heel height), and across the catalogue there are about {{attribute_names}} distinct attribute names, added by merchandisers every week. Customers write reviews and questions without limit. The storefront reads the catalogue at about {{peak_reads}} reads per second at peak, mostly product pages and filtered category listings ("waterproof hiking boots, size 44, under 120"). Stock changes every few seconds on popular items. Analysts want price history and the share of products missing key attributes per category.
sections.problem: Design the collections and documents: what is embedded in a product document and what is referenced, how variants are stored, how the open-ended attributes are represented so that category filters can use indexes, where reviews and stock live, and how price changes keep their history. Give the indexes for the product page, the filtered listing and the merchandiser's "products missing attribute X" report. Say what you validate at write time, and how the catalogue reaches the analytics store.
sections.constraints: One document stays well below the document size limit (16 MB in this exercise; check current docs) for the largest product. A product page needs one read in the common case. A filter on any attribute name and value is served by an index, not a collection scan. A price shown on the product page must match the price charged at checkout. Stock updates on a popular item must not rewrite the whole product document.
sections.assumptions: Catalogue size, variant counts, attribute counts and read rates are hypothetical. Prices are integers in minor units with a currency. A merchandiser can add an attribute name without a deployment. Search ranking is out of scope; filtering and the product page are in scope.
sections.criteria: Embedding chosen by read pattern, size bound and change rate, with an estimate for the largest product; variants embedded with a stated cut-over, or referenced with a summary kept on the product; attributes as name/value pairs (or a wildcard index, with its limits stated) with one compound index; reviews and questions referenced, with a small embedded subset for the page; stock separated from slowly changing product data; price consistency with checkout; schema validation for types and required fields; price history and analytics through change streams or exports; each incident contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: How many reviews does a popular product get?
clarifications.a: Tens of thousands, and they keep coming. The product page shows a rating summary and the newest five.

clarifications.q: Do variants share attributes?
clarifications.a: Most attributes belong to the product; size, colour and material vary per variant, and a few categories have more variant-level attributes.

clarifications.q: Can one attribute have values of different types?
clarifications.a: Yes, merchandisers have entered "15" and 15 for the same attribute in different products. Say what you enforce.

clarifications.q: How fresh must stock be on the product page?
clarifications.a: Within a few seconds. "In stock" shown for an item that sold out a minute ago is a complaint.

clarifications.q: Do analysts query the operational cluster?
clarifications.a: Not for heavy work. They have a warehouse; say how data gets there.

hints: Embed what is read together and bounded in size; reference what grows without limit or changes at a different rate.
Open-ended attributes become an array of name/value pairs, and one compound index on the pair serves every attribute filter.
Look at which index fields are arrays. A compound index can have at most one field that is an array in any one document (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
followups: Estimate the size of your largest product document with {{max_variants}} variants. At what point do you move variants out, and what does the product page read then?
Write the index and the query for "waterproof = true, size = 44, price below 120" when waterproof is a product attribute and size and price are per variant.
Stock changes every few seconds on popular items. Where does stock live, and how does the listing filter "in stock only" stay correct without hot updates on the product document?
A merchandiser renames attribute "colour" to "color" across 3 million products. How does that run, and what do filters return during it?

Prices change and the warehouse needs price history per SKU. Do you keep history in the operational document, in a separate collection, or only downstream from a change stream? Defend it at {{peak_reads}} reads per second.

rules.ask: A product collects tens of thousands of reviews. What happens to the document, its size and every write to it after a year? Which reviews would you keep in the product, if any?
Show the compound index on the pairs. How does it treat "15" and 15, and how do you filter on two attributes at once?
When is a wildcard index the better choice than the attribute pattern, and what do you lose in a query that filters on two attributes?
The product page is the hottest read. How many collections does it touch now, and what do you denormalise to make it one read?
The product page now needs every variant. How many reads is that, and how do you keep the product's price range and "in stock" flag consistent with the variants?

incidents: A supplier feed creates a product with {{max_variants}} variants, each embedding images and translations; inserts start failing on the document size limit, and the import job retries forever, blocking the feed for every other supplier.

After variant-level size and product-level tags were both stored as arrays, building a compound index on them fails, because some documents have both as arrays; the release that needed the index had already shipped.
During a sale, one popular product's document is updated hundreds of times a second for stock; writes on it conflict and retry, and product page reads for it see latency spikes.

templates.title: Time-series collections for device readings — metadata, granularity, buckets, late data and retention
templates.subtopic: metaField, granularity and bucket sizing, late arrivals, downsampling, retention

sections.scenario: A company makes connected industrial sensors and stores their readings in time-series collections of a document database. About {{devices}} devices each send a reading every {{interval}}: a timestamp, the device id, a few measurements (temperature, vibration, power) and some metadata that rarely changes (site, device model, firmware version). Devices on poor networks buffer readings and upload them later; about {{late_share}} of readings arrive more than an hour after they were taken, some a few days late. Customers look at a device's last hour in a dashboard, compare sites over months, and receive alerts. Raw readings are kept for {{retention_days}} days; customers want trends for years.
sections.problem: Design the storage: the time field, what goes into the metaField and what stays a measurement, the granularity or bucket settings for this reading rate, the secondary indexes, and how the collection is sharded if it needs to be. Then design the rest of the read path: the "latest reading per device" lookup, hourly and daily rollups, how late readings reach rollups that were already computed, and retention for raw data and for each rollup. Estimate readings per bucket and the write rate.
sections.constraints: The dashboard's last-hour query for one device returns in under 100 ms. Readings older than {{retention_days}} days are deleted automatically. A late reading is never dropped while it is younger than the retention period, and the rollups that cover it are corrected. Metadata changes (a device moved to another site) must not rewrite historical readings.
sections.assumptions: Device counts, rates, shares and the retention are hypothetical. In this exercise, a time-series collection groups readings into buckets by metaField value and time span, granularity or custom bucket settings bound a bucket's span, and expireAfterSeconds deletes whole buckets once all their readings are old enough (this exercise's rules; check current docs for the current behaviour and limits).
sections.criteria: metaField limited to stable series identity, measurements as fields, granularity matched to {{interval}} with a readings-per-bucket estimate; indexes for per-device and per-site queries; a "latest reading" collection updated on write; rollups recomputed for the time ranges that late readings touch, idempotently; retention per tier with the expiry semantics of buckets explained; site and firmware handled as time-varying attributes; bad clocks quarantined; sharding justified by write rate with a key that keeps per-device queries targeted; each incident contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does the firmware version belong in the metaField?
clarifications.a: Your call. It changes a few times a year per device; say what that does to the buckets.

clarifications.q: Can a reading be corrected after it is written?
clarifications.a: Rarely, by a calibration job. Say how, given that updates to time-series data are restricted in this exercise.

clarifications.q: How late is too late?
clarifications.a: A reading older than the retention period on arrival is dropped and counted. Anything younger must be stored.

clarifications.q: Do customers query across devices?
clarifications.a: Yes, by site and model: "average vibration per site per day for the last quarter".

clarifications.q: Is the clock on the device trustworthy?
clarifications.a: Mostly. Some devices reboot with a clock in 1970 until they sync; say what you do with those.

hints: The metaField decides which readings share a bucket. Put there what identifies the series and rarely changes; a value that differs per reading creates a bucket per reading.
Choose granularity from the interval: a bucket should hold many readings from one series, not one reading or a whole year.
The "latest reading" and long-term trends are different access patterns; serve them from their own small collections, kept up to date as readings arrive.
followups: At {{devices}} devices every {{interval}}, how many readings a second do you insert, and roughly how many readings land in one bucket with your settings?
A reading arrives three days late. Which bucket does it go to, what does it cost, and how does the daily rollup for that day get corrected?
Devices move between sites. Your rollup per site per day was computed with the old site. What should "average per site" mean for last month, and how do you produce it?
Raw data expires after {{retention_days}} days. What prevents a rollup from losing late readings that arrive just before their raw data expires?
Would you shard this collection, and on what? Show what a site-wide query and the per-device dashboard each touch.

rules.ask: Firmware version is also in your metaField. What happens to the bucket for a device on the day its firmware changes, and to a query across firmware versions?
If that identifier is in the metaField, how many readings share a bucket? What does that do to storage and compression?
With readings every {{interval}}, how many readings fit in one bucket with that setting, and why does that number matter?
Expiry removes a whole bucket only when its newest reading is old enough. How late can a reading be deleted, and does a late reading extend its bucket's life?
The hourly rollup already ran when a late reading arrives. Which run picks it up, and how do you make re-running an hour idempotent?

incidents: A firmware release starts sending a per-reading message id inside the device metadata; the ingest service copies it into the metaField, every reading becomes its own bucket, and storage for those devices grows tens of times within a day.

A cellular outage at a large site ends and its devices upload six days of buffered readings at once; with {{late_share}} of readings already late on a normal day, the hourly rollups for the past week are now wrong and an alert threshold fires on stale data.

Devices that rebooted with their clock at 1970 wrote readings that are already older than {{retention_days}} days; they were expired almost immediately, and with them a calibration record the customer needed.

templates.title: Shard key choice for a multi-tenant application — tenant prefixes, hashing, jumbo chunks and zones for residency
templates.subtopic: shard key, targeted versus scatter-gather queries, jumbo chunks, zones for data residency

sections.scenario: A business software company runs a multi-tenant application on a sharded document database. Each of its {{tenants}} customer tenants has users, projects and an activity feed; the activity collection takes about {{writes_per_second}} inserts a second and is read as "the latest activity in this project" and "all activity for this tenant last week". Tenants vary enormously: the largest holds about {{largest_tenant_share}} of all activity. Contracts require some tenants' data to stay in a chosen region; the cluster has shards in {{regions}} regions. Tenants occasionally move to another region, and large tenants occasionally ask for an export of everything.
sections.problem: Choose the shard key for activity (and say whether projects and users need to be sharded at all). Compare at least three candidates — the tenant id alone, the tenant id plus a hashed or time-ordered suffix, and a hashed id — on write distribution, targeted reads, chunk splitting for the largest tenant, and data residency. Show how zones pin residency tenants to their region's shards, what happens when a tenant changes region, and what you monitor to know the key is still right a year from now.
sections.constraints: No single shard takes more than a fair share of inserts at peak. "Latest activity in a project" is a targeted query (one shard), not scatter-gather. A residency tenant's documents never sit on a shard outside its region, including during a move. The shard key cannot be changed casually: changing it means resharding the collection (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
sections.assumptions: Tenant counts, shares, regions and rates are hypothetical. Document _ids are time-ordered identifiers generated by the application. In this exercise the balancer moves chunks between shards, cannot split a chunk whose documents all share one shard key value (a jumbo chunk), and zones map shard key ranges to sets of shards (this exercise's rules; check current docs).
sections.criteria: Explicit criteria for a shard key (cardinality, frequency, monotonicity, targeting) applied to each candidate; a tenant-prefixed compound key with a suffix that splits large tenants, or a hashed design with its read cost stated; jumbo chunks and hot chunks explained; unsharded small collections where appropriate; zones expressed as key ranges with a region-change runbook; email lookup through a small index collection; monitoring of chunk and data distribution, scatter-gather share and per-shard write load; refine, reshard or dedicated cluster chosen by stated thresholds; each incident contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Do queries always include the tenant id?
clarifications.a: Every application query does. Internal support tools sometimes search by user email across tenants.

clarifications.q: Can a tenant's region change?
clarifications.a: Yes, a few times a month across all tenants, on request, with a deadline.

clarifications.q: Is hashed _id alone acceptable?
clarifications.a: It spreads writes perfectly. Tell me what it does to "latest activity in a project".

clarifications.q: How big can one tenant's data get?
clarifications.a: The largest is about {{largest_tenant_share}} of the collection and growing.

clarifications.q: Are cross-tenant analytics run here?
clarifications.a: No, they run on a warehouse copy. The cluster serves the application.

hints: A shard key should give enough distinct values, an even write spread and targeted reads for the main queries. A key whose leading field is the tenant gives targeting; a suffix gives the largest tenant room to split.
A monotonically increasing key sends every insert to the chunk holding the maximum; hashing that part spreads inserts, at the cost of range reads on it.
Zones work on ranges of the shard key, so a residency rule must be expressible as a key prefix: put what decides residency at the front of the key, or map tenants to ranges.
followups: With {tenant_id} alone, what happens to the largest tenant's chunks, and to the shard that holds them?
Compare {tenant_id, project_id, _id} with {tenant_id, hashed _id} for "latest activity in this project" and for insert distribution.
A residency tenant moves from one region to another with a deadline in two weeks. Walk through the zone change, the data movement, and what the tenant's users see during it.
Support searches by user email across tenants. How do you serve that without scatter-gather on activity at {{writes_per_second}} inserts a second?

A year later, the largest tenant is twice its size and a quarter of all chunks are on one region's shards. What signals told you, and do you refine the key, reshard, or move the tenant to its own cluster?

rules.ask: Every query now goes to every shard unless it carries the exact _id. What does "latest activity in a project" cost at your shard count?
The largest tenant holds {{largest_tenant_share}} of the data, all with one key value. Can its chunks split, and where do its writes go?
A time-ordered suffix keeps new documents together. Which chunk gets every new insert for the largest tenant, and how does that shard cope?
Zones map key ranges to shards. What exactly is the range for one residency tenant, and what happens to its documents while the zone is being changed?
Which tenants get their own cluster, decided by what rule, and what does that do to the application's routing and to cross-tenant support tools?

incidents: With the key on the tenant id alone, the largest tenant (about {{largest_tenant_share}} of the data) ends up in chunks that cannot be split; the balancer cannot move them, and one shard runs out of disk while the others have plenty.

A key of {tenant_id, _id} with time-ordered ids sends every new activity of the largest tenant to the last chunk of its range; at peak that shard's write latency climbs while the rest of the cluster is idle.

A residency tenant's region change is applied by editing the zone ranges during peak hours; migrations of its chunks compete with application writes, and for a while the tenant's documents exist in two regions at once.

templates.title: Documents at several schema versions — migrate on read, backfill in place, and analytics over mixed versions
templates.subtopic: schema version field, lazy and background migration, throttled backfills, versioned analytics

sections.scenario: A subscription business keeps its accounts collection in a document database: about {{documents}} documents, each holding a customer's profile, plan, billing settings and addresses. Over the years the shape changed several times: prices moved from a decimal amount in dollars to integer cents with a currency, a single address became a list of addresses with types, and plan fields moved into a nested document. Today {{versions_live}} versions of the document live side by side, because older ones were never rewritten. About {{daily_touched}} of documents are written on a normal day. A change stream feeds the warehouse, where analysts compute revenue and plan mix. The team wants to stop carrying old versions in application code within {{backfill_days}} days.
sections.problem: Design schema versioning for this collection: how a document records its version, how the application reads and writes every live version, and how old documents are upgraded — on read, on write, by a background backfill, or a combination. Design the backfill so it does not hurt the production workload or replication. Then design the analytics side: how the warehouse turns mixed versions into one model, how it learns that a new version exists, and how a release that needs to be rolled back is made safe for documents already written in the new shape.
sections.constraints: No document is lost or silently truncated by an upgrade. The application can be rolled back one release at any time. The backfill keeps replication lag on secondaries under a stated budget and never makes a secondary fall off the end of the oplog (a capped log of a fixed size in this exercise; check current docs). Revenue in the warehouse is correct for every day, whichever version the documents were in.
sections.assumptions: Document counts, versions, touch rates and the deadline are hypothetical. Each document has an immutable _id. In this exercise, a change stream delivers every insert, update and replace with a resume token, and an update to one field is delivered as an update description unless the full document is requested (this exercise's rules; check current docs).
sections.criteria: An explicit, indexed schema version; read and write paths that handle every live version; upgrade on write plus a resumable, throttled backfill with conditional updates; lag and oplog-window guardrails; a proof of completion (count by version reaching zero); forward-compatible releases (preserve unknown fields, expand then contract) so rollback is safe; a versioned mapping into one warehouse model with unknown versions rejected; reconciliation of totals across versions; each incident contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is there a version field today?
clarifications.a: Only on the newest version. Older documents must be recognised by their shape; say how reliably.

clarifications.q: Can the backfill run at full speed at night?
clarifications.a: Traffic is global, so there is no quiet night. Say what you throttle on.

clarifications.q: Does the warehouse see full documents?
clarifications.a: It sees change events; ask for what you need and say what it costs.

clarifications.q: What happens if two writers update a document while it is being upgraded?
clarifications.a: That is your problem to prevent: the upgrade must not overwrite a concurrent change.

clarifications.q: How do we know when old versions are gone?
clarifications.a: Your design should be able to prove it.

hints: Make the version explicit and indexed. Detect shapes once, write the version number, and never rely on detection afterwards.

Upgrade on write is free for touched documents; the backfill is only for the untouched tail. Make each upgrade a conditional update on the version it read, so a concurrent writer wins and the backfill retries.
In the warehouse, normalise every version into one model with an explicit mapping per version, and fail loudly on an unknown version instead of guessing.
followups: With {{daily_touched}} of documents written a day, how many remain at old versions after {{backfill_days}} days without a backfill? What does that say about the backfill's size?
Write the upgrade of one document from dollars to cents as a conditional update. What happens if the customer changes plan at the same moment?
The backfill runs in batches. What do you throttle on, how do you resume after a crash, and how do you prove at the end that no old version remains?
A release that writes a new version is rolled back after two hours. What does the previous release do with documents in the new shape, and how do you avoid losing their new fields?
Analysts report revenue doubled on one day. Walk through how mixed versions in the change stream could cause that, and the guard that would have caught it.

rules.ask: Reads now write. What does that do to read latency, to secondaries serving reads, and to documents that are never read?
How big is each batch, what do you throttle on, and what happens to replication lag and the oplog window while it runs?
With {{versions_live}} versions live, what does your validator accept today, and when do you tighten it to the newest version only?
An update event carries only the changed fields. How does the warehouse know which version the document is in, and what does requesting the full document cost?
The old release reads a document in the new shape and writes it back. Which fields survive, and how do you design the release so that this is safe?

incidents: An unthrottled backfill rewrites documents as fast as the primary allows; replication lag on one secondary grows past the oplog window, the secondary stops replicating and needs a full resync, and the replica set runs for a day with less redundancy.

After the move from dollars to cents, the warehouse's revenue for one day is 100 times too high for part of the accounts: the mapping was keyed on a field that both versions have, and {{versions_live}} versions were live that day.

A release writing a new address shape is rolled back; the previous release reads those documents, does not recognise the new field and writes the documents back without it, and customers' new addresses disappear.

templates.title: Chunk ownership by hour — reconstructing a sharded collection's layout from split and migration events
templates.subtopic: state reconstruction from an event log, hours with no events, empty shards, boundaries

sections.scenario: A sharded cluster spreads the collection {{ns}} across shards in chunks: contiguous ranges of the shard key. A chunk that grows is split into smaller chunks, and the balancer migrates chunks between shards to even them out. Every split and migration is written to a changelog, which is exported to the warehouse as chunk_events; the cluster's shards ({{shard_list}}) are listed in shards with the time each was added. {{late_note}} The platform team wants to see, hour by hour, how the chunks of {{ns}} were spread and whether the spread crossed the exercise's balancing threshold.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns one row for every hour from {{window_start}} up to, but not including, {{window_end}} ({{hours}} rows, ordered by hour_start), describing the layout at the end of that hour: hour_start, active_shards, total_chunks, max_chunks, min_chunks, imbalance, most_loaded_shard, needs_balancing. The layout at the end of an hour applies every event with occurred_at strictly before the next hour starts; an event exactly on the boundary belongs to the next hour. {{kinds_rule}} A chunk exists from the event that creates it until a later event names it as source_chunk_id; its owner is the shard_id of its latest create, split, merge or move_commit event. Active shards are those with added_at strictly before the end of the hour, and an active shard with no chunks counts with 0. total_chunks counts each chunk of the collection once; max_chunks and min_chunks are over the active shards; imbalance is max_chunks − min_chunks; most_loaded_shard is the active shard with the most chunks, ties going to the smallest shard_id. {{threshold_rule}} {{ns_rule}}
