sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every hour of the window appears, including hours in which nothing happened. The sample has {{events}} event rows; production keeps months of changelog for thousands of collections.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, shard names, collections and times. The threshold rule is this exercise's own: this exercise measures balance in chunk counts, as older balancer versions did, while current versions balance by data size (check current docs). A split's shard_id is the shard that owned the chunk when it was split, so no ownership has to be inherited recursively.
sections.criteria: Hours generated rather than taken from events; chunk existence from creating and source events, with split and merge sources retired; owner from create, split, merge and committed migrations only; strict boundary at the hour's end; empty active shards counted through a LEFT JOIN, and shards counted only once added; at Hard and above, only the named collection and only committed migrations; at Very Hard, a merged chunk counted once; deterministic tie rule and threshold; can explain interval-based scaling, a baseline snapshot for a capped changelog, and data-size balance.

clarifications.q: Does a migration committed at exactly 10:00:00 count in the 09:00 hour?
clarifications.a: No. The 09:00 row shows the layout just before 10:00:00; that migration first appears in the 10:00 row.

clarifications.q: Does a shard with no chunks count in min_chunks?
clarifications.a: Yes, once it has been added. A new shard at 0 chunks is exactly what the team wants to see.

clarifications.q: What owns a chunk that was created by a split?
clarifications.a: The shard_id on the split row, until a committed migration moves it.

clarifications.q: Do I need the chunk key ranges?
clarifications.a: No. Ownership and existence are enough for this report.

clarifications.q: What if an hour has no events at all?
clarifications.a: It still gets a row; the layout carries over from the previous hour.

hints: Build the hours first (generate_series), then compute each chunk's state as of each hour's end. A cross join of hours and chunks is small here.
For each chunk: when it was created, when (if ever) it was split or merged away, and its owner as of a time — the latest ownership event before that time.
Count per active shard with a LEFT JOIN from shards, so empty shards stay in, then aggregate per hour. DISTINCT ON picks one shard per hour for the tie rule.
followups: At months of changelog for thousands of collections, a cross join of hours and chunks gets expensive. How would you compute ownership intervals once (with LEAD) and join hours to intervals instead?
The changelog is capped and its oldest events have rolled off. How do you get a starting layout so that the reconstruction still works?
Change imbalance to data size per shard instead of chunk counts. What would you need in the changelog, and why can a shard with fewer chunks still be the fullest?
Write the follow-on query that lists, for the latest hour, the chunks that would have to move to bring every shard within the threshold.

rules.ask: Grouping events by the hour they happened in counts what changed in that hour. The report needs the whole layout at the end of each hour, including quiet hours. How do you carry state forward?
Which shard disappears from your counts when it has no chunks yet, and what does that do to min_chunks for a shard that was just added?
How many rows does one merge write for its new chunk? Is your count of chunks or of rows?
The latest migration row for a chunk is an abort. Who owns the chunk now?
Your interval for an ownership ends at the next event. Is that end inclusive or exclusive, and which hour does an event at exactly hh:00:00 land in?
Does any owner here have to be inherited from a parent chunk? Look at what the split row already tells you.

incidents: The changelog is a capped collection in this exercise (check current docs); on a day of heavy splitting the oldest create and split rows for {{ns}} rolled off before the export ran, and the reconstruction found migrations of chunks it had never seen created.

A dashboard built on this query paged on-call every hour after a new shard was added, because min_chunks stayed at 0 while the balancer was still filling it; nobody had decided whether a shard that is filling counts towards the alert.

During a config server failover, a migration's move_start was exported but its outcome row arrived an hour later; a version of this report that took the latest migration row as the owner showed the chunk on its destination shard, and an operator drained the wrong shard.

templates.title: Cluster performance telemetry for many thousands of clusters
templates.subtopic: per-member metrics, rollups, replication-lag and disk alerts

sections.scenario: A managed document-database service runs {{clusters}} customer clusters. Each is a replica set of three, five or seven members, or a sharded cluster made of several replica-set shards, config servers and query routers. An agent beside every member reports metrics every {{sample_seconds}} seconds: operation counters, read and write latencies, connections, cache usage, replication lag, the oplog window, disk used and free, and CPU. Customers see charts for their own clusters in the console and set alerts on them; the service's on-call engineers also need fleet-wide views. Clusters change shape all the time: members are replaced, tiers are resized by rolling restarts, shards are added.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry platform: collection and ingestion, the storage layout for raw samples and rollups, the read paths for one cluster's charts and for fleet-wide questions ("which clusters have the largest replication lag right now?"), alert evaluation that notifies within {{alert_minutes}} minutes of a condition holding, retention for {{retention_days}} days, and isolation so one customer can never see another's metrics. Say how you handle counters that reset when a member restarts, members that come and go, and samples that arrive late.
sections.constraints: A chart of one cluster over the last week loads in under 2 seconds. An alert fires within {{alert_minutes}} minutes of its condition first holding, and a missing sample is never treated as a zero. Metrics are billed to no one, so storage cost per cluster must stay flat as the fleet grows. A member's metrics are shown under the cluster it belonged to at the time of the sample.
sections.assumptions: All counts, intervals and thresholds are hypothetical. For this exercise: operation counters are cumulative since the member process started and reset to zero on restart; replication lag of a secondary is the primary's latest operation time minus the secondary's latest applied operation time; an idle primary writes a no-op entry to the oplog every 10 seconds; the oplog window is the time span between the oldest and newest entries in a fixed-size oplog. These are this exercise's rules; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Stable member identity with topology as time-bounded events; counter-reset-aware rate computation at ingestion; a hot recent store for raw samples and alert evaluation, and a columnar or time-series history with rollups chosen per metric (sums and counts for rates, histograms or sketches for latency); alert evaluation as incremental state per rule and series, event-time windows with explicit no-data handling; lag semantics that account for idle primaries; tenant isolation enforced on every read path; per-tenant query quotas; cost per cluster kept flat; retention for {{retention_days}} days by tier; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do customers define their own alert thresholds?
clarifications.a: Yes, per cluster, on any metric, with a duration ("lag above 30 s for 3 minutes"). The service also has its own fleet alerts.

clarifications.q: Is per-second resolution needed?
clarifications.a: No. Raw samples at {{sample_seconds}} seconds for recent data; coarser rollups beyond that are your choice.

clarifications.q: Can an agent buffer when it cannot reach ingestion?
clarifications.a: Yes, for about an hour on local disk, and then it drops the oldest samples.

clarifications.q: Are clusters in many cloud regions?
clarifications.a: Yes. Metrics may be stored centrally or per region; say which and why.

clarifications.q: Do customers export metrics to their own tools?
clarifications.a: Some do, through an API that reads the same store as the charts.

hints: Key everything by a stable member identity plus the cluster it belonged to at the time; topology changes are events, not overwrites.
Turn cumulative counters into rates at ingestion, detecting resets, rather than at query time.
Alerting and charting want different stores: one evaluates recent windows continuously, the other scans history.
followups: Walk through one sample from the agent to a customer's chart and to an alert decision. Where is it stored, keyed how, and rolled up when?
A secondary is replaced by a new member during a tier change. What does the replication-lag chart for that cluster show across the change?
How do you evaluate tens of thousands of customer alert rules every {{sample_seconds}} seconds without scanning the raw store?
Disk alerts should warn before a disk fills, not when it is full. How do you project time to full, and what makes that projection lie?
How do you keep one noisy cluster, or one customer's export job, from slowing every other customer's charts?

rules.ask: How many distinct series is that across {{clusters}} clusters, and what happens to your store when a cluster with hundreds of shards is added?
A member restarts between two samples. What does your rate show for that interval, and how do you know it was a restart rather than a real drop?
Agents in one region reconnect after 40 minutes and flush their buffers at once. What does your alert evaluator see, and in what order?
Which aggregate do you keep for latency in an hourly rollup, and can you still answer "p99 over the day" from it?
Where is the customer id checked on a chart request, and what stops the fleet-wide view from leaking into a customer's API?

incidents: During a fleet-wide rolling upgrade every member restarts once. Operations-per-second charts show huge negative spikes, and the fleet view of "busiest clusters" is topped by clusters that were idle.
A customer's idle cluster shows replication lag swinging between 0 and 10 seconds, and their alert at 5 seconds of lag for 1 minute pages them every few minutes all night.

Agents in one region lose their connection to ingestion for 40 minutes and then flush their buffers. Their samples arrive late and out of order, and alerts that should have fired at {{alert_minutes}} minutes fire 40 minutes late or not at all.

A disk projection based on the last hour's growth fires "disk full in 3 hours" for hundreds of clusters during a nightly index build that frees its temporary space when it finishes, and on-call starts ignoring the alert.

templates.title: Online resharding: changing a live collection's shard key
templates.subtopic: online resharding, catch-up, cutover, verification

sections.scenario: A customer's orders collection of {{collection_tb}} TB is sharded across {{shards}} shards on a key of {region: 1}. It was a reasonable choice when the company had a few large regions; now one region holds most of the orders, its chunks cannot be split any further, and one shard takes most of the {{writes_per_s}} writes per second at peak. The customer wants to move to a compound key of the tenant id and a hashed order id, without taking the application offline.
sections.problem: Design the online resharding process the database service runs for the customer. Cover how documents are copied into the layout of the new key while the application keeps writing; how changes made during the copy are captured and applied; how and when the cluster switches from the old layout to the new one, blocking writes to the collection for at most {{block_seconds}} seconds; how you verify the new layout before and after the switch; how the operation can be aborted at any point before the switch with the old layout intact; and what the customer sees and must do.
sections.constraints: Writes may be blocked for at most {{block_seconds}} seconds, once. Reads never fail because of the operation. No write acknowledged with majority write concern may be lost. The extra disk and I/O load must not push the cluster's ordinary p99 latency above twice its normal value. Unique indexes stay enforced throughout.
sections.assumptions: All sizes and rates are hypothetical. For this exercise: each shard's oplog is a fixed-size log, so it covers only a limited window of time; the copy is driven from a cluster time recorded at the start; resharding needs free disk space on the receiving shards roughly equal to the collection's size; routers learn the collection's layout from metadata held by the config servers. These are this exercise's rules; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Three clear phases (consistent copy at a cluster time, oplog-driven catch-up, a bounded commit); an oplog-window check before and during the copy, with resizing or faster copy as remedies; idempotent change application and correct handling of transactions and retried writes across the switch (session and retry history carried to the new owner); a commit gate based on measured catch-up rate against {{block_seconds}} seconds, with deferral at peak; atomic metadata switch with router refresh; verification by per-range counts and hashes at the same cluster time plus sampling; abort leaves the old layout untouched and cleans up; change-stream continuity explained; resource controls; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can we add shards for the duration?
clarifications.a: Yes, at a cost the customer pays; say whether you would and why.

clarifications.q: Does the application use multi-document transactions?
clarifications.a: Some writes do, across orders and order lines in the same collection.

clarifications.q: Do applications retry writes?
clarifications.a: Yes; their drivers retry a failed write once, and they rely on a retried write not being applied twice.

clarifications.q: Are there change-stream consumers on the collection?
clarifications.a: Yes, an analytics pipeline that resumes from stored resume tokens.

clarifications.q: Can the customer choose when the switch happens?
clarifications.a: Your design should say whether it is automatic, scheduled or approved by the customer.

hints: Separate the operation into a bulk copy as of one cluster time, a catch-up that applies every change since that time, and a short, bounded switch.
The catch-up reads the source shards' oplogs. Compare the copy's duration with how much time those oplogs cover.
The switch is a metadata change on the config servers. Decide what must be true before it is allowed to commit.
followups: Walk through a single order document that is updated twice during the copy and once during the switch. Where is each change applied, and what guarantees it is applied once?
How do you decide that the catch-up is close enough to start the {{block_seconds}}-second switch, and what happens if peak traffic arrives just then?
A write is retried by a driver after the switch, but the first attempt was applied on the old layout. How does the new owner know not to apply it again?
How do you verify, before committing, that the new layout holds exactly the documents of the old one, without reading {{collection_tb}} TB twice?
What happens to the analytics pipeline's change stream across the switch, and to a resume token issued before it?

rules.ask: The copy of {{collection_tb}} TB takes longer than one shard's oplog covers at peak. What does your process do when it finds the oplog entry it needs is gone?
Who performs the dual writes, the routers or the application, and what happens to a transaction that touches documents mapped to two different new owners?
Documents keep changing while you compute your hashes. At which cluster time are the old and new hashes taken, and how do you compare them?
The operation aborts after the receiving shards have used most of their free disk. What is cleaned up, in what order, and what does the customer pay for?
Throttling the copy keeps latency safe but makes it take three days. What does that do to your catch-up and to the oplog window?

incidents: The copy of {{collection_tb}} TB takes 31 hours because of throttling, but one source shard's oplog covers only 26 hours at peak. At catch-up, that shard's oldest needed entry has been overwritten.

When the switch is due, peak traffic of {{writes_per_s}} writes per second means the receivers fall further behind each minute, and the remaining changes cannot be applied within {{block_seconds}} seconds.

Seconds before the switch, the order service increments an order's item count; the reply is lost and the driver retries after the switch. The retry is applied again on the new owner, and the customer is charged for one item more than they ordered.

A nightly report that counts orders per tenant shows 0.03% more documents than the application's own totals for a day after the switch, until a cleanup removes leftover copies on shards that no longer own them.

templates.title: Multi-region replica sets: placement, write concern and regional failure
templates.subtopic: multi-region replica sets, elections, write concern, read preference

regions: two regions on one continent, about 15 ms apart
three regions on one continent, up to 40 ms apart
two continents with two regions each, about 80 ms apart across the ocean
loss_rule: no acknowledged order may ever be lost
no acknowledged order may be lost; activity-feed writes may lose a few seconds

sections.scenario: A retailer runs its order and activity-feed data in one replica set and serves customers from {{regions}} in round-trip time. The workload is {{read_mix}}, mostly customers viewing their own orders and feeds. The business rule is that {{loss_rule}}. Last year a cloud region was unavailable for six hours, and the retailer now wants the database to survive the loss of any one region with automatic failover.
sections.problem: Design the deployment. Cover how many members go in which regions and why, member priorities and votes, any members that should not become primary or should not serve reads, the write concern per kind of write, the read preference and read concern per kind of read, and how a customer always sees an order they just placed. Then walk through, step by step, what the application sees when the region holding the primary is lost, and when that region is only cut off from the others.
sections.constraints: Survive the loss of any one region with a new primary within one minute and no manual step. Honour the loss rule above. Order placement p99 under 300 ms from any customer location. Customers must see their own new order on their next page view.
sections.assumptions: All latencies and workloads are hypothetical. For this exercise: a replica set has at most 7 voting members; a primary needs to see a majority of voting members or it steps down; an election starts after the primary has been unreachable for about 10 seconds; a write acknowledged by only the primary can be rolled back if that primary fails before the write reaches a majority; an arbiter votes but holds no data. These are this exercise's rules; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Member placement where losing any region leaves a voting majority (a third site for a tie-breaker when only two serving regions exist); priorities that prefer the serving regions and avoid electing a far member; majority write concern for orders, with any weaker concern limited to data the loss rule allows to lose; read preferences per read with bounded staleness, and read-your-own-writes through the primary or causally consistent sessions carrying the operation time across servers; clear accounting of inter-region round trips per write; correct election and step-down behaviour under loss and partition; arbiters and hidden or delayed members used knowingly; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is a third site available for a tie-breaking member?
clarifications.a: Yes, in any region, at a cost; say what you would put there.

clarifications.q: Can the application be in all regions?
clarifications.a: Yes; application servers run in every serving region, and each talks to the whole replica set.

clarifications.q: Do drivers retry writes?
clarifications.a: Yes, once, on errors that are safe to retry.

clarifications.q: Is the activity feed in the same collections as orders?
clarifications.a: Separate collections in the same replica set.

clarifications.q: Would sharding by region be acceptable?
clarifications.a: Not in this round. One replica set; you can mention when you would change that.

hints: Count votes per region first: after losing any one region, do the survivors hold a majority?
A write is safe from rollback only once a majority holds it. Work out where that majority is and what it costs in round trips.
Reading your own write needs either the primary or a session that carries the time of the write.
followups: Show the member layout and the vote count left after losing each region in turn.
What does an order placement cost in round trips with your write concern, and how does it change after a failover moves the primary?
The primary's region is cut off but still running, with application servers that customers can reach. What happens to writes and reads there, minute by minute?
How does a customer in a far region see their own order immediately while most reads go to a nearby secondary?
Where would you use an arbiter, a hidden member or a delayed member here, and where would each one hurt you?

rules.ask: One data-bearing secondary goes down for maintenance while the arbiter is up. What happens to your majority writes and to the primary's memory?
Which writes use that, and what happens to them if the primary fails one second after acknowledging?
A secondary is 20 seconds behind. Which customers see stale data, and what bounds it?
The highest-priority member's region comes back after the failover. Does it take the primary back, and what does the application feel when it does?
The customer's next page view lands on a different application server in another region. Does the session's time travel with it?

incidents: A configuration change sets the default write concern to acknowledgement by the primary alone, to cut order latency. A month later the primary fails; on its return about 4 seconds of acknowledged orders are rolled back and set aside, against the rule that {{loss_rule}}.

A three-member layout with an arbiter in the cheapest region is chosen to save cost. While the one data-bearing secondary is down for an upgrade, majority writes time out, the application's retries pile up, and the primary's cache fills with changes it cannot yet consider committed.

The primary's region is cut off from the others for 12 minutes but stays reachable from customers there. The old primary steps down; customers in that region can still read from local secondaries and see orders that stop updating, while a new primary is elected in another region.

After the failover, every write from the application servers in the original region, and each retry, now crosses an inter-region link before it is even sent to a majority, and order placement p99 there rises by several of those round trips until traffic is moved.

templates.title: Customer-managed encryption keys: rotation, revocation, backups and replicas
templates.subtopic: envelope encryption, key rotation and revocation, backups

sections.scenario: A managed database service lets customers encrypt their clusters at rest with a key they hold in their own cloud provider's key management service. {{clusters}} clusters use the feature, some spread across regions. Customers rotate their key every {{rotation_days}} days, keep backups for {{backup_days}} days, and expect that if they revoke the service's access to their key, their data stops being readable by anyone within {{revoke_hours}} hours. Auditors ask every customer to prove both: rotations happen, and revocation works.
sections.problem: Design how customer-managed keys are used. Cover the key hierarchy (what the customer's key encrypts, and what encrypts the data files); how a cluster member gets the keys it needs when it starts, restarts or is replaced; key rotation, and whether it rewrites data; how backups and snapshots are encrypted and what a restore needs; what happens to replicas in other regions; how the service detects that access has been revoked and what it does then; and the audit trail a customer can show their auditors.
sections.constraints: The service never holds the customer's key material in plaintext outside the key management service. Rotation must not take a cluster offline. A restore of any backup within {{backup_days}} days must work, or fail with a clear reason the customer can act on. After revocation, no member, backup or restore can decrypt data within {{revoke_hours}} hours.
sections.assumptions: All counts and periods are hypothetical. For this exercise: the key management service lets an authorised caller ask it to encrypt or decrypt a small key with the customer's key, logs every such call in the customer's account, and keeps previous key versions until the customer deletes them; the database's storage engine encrypts data files with its own data keys, which can be wrapped by a master key. These are this exercise's rules; check current docs.
sections.criteria: A clear envelope hierarchy (customer key wraps per-cluster or per-member data keys; data keys encrypt files) with plaintext customer key never leaving the key service; member start and replacement paths with least-privilege access; rotation by rewrapping, propagated to every member and region, with optional re-encryption as a separate, scheduled operation; a per-backup record of the key versions it depends on, with warnings and blocks before a customer deletes a version a retained backup needs; revocation detected by periodic and event-driven checks, distinguished from outages, with a bounded in-memory key lifetime and a defined shutdown sequence within {{revoke_hours}} hours; replicas and exports covered; auditable evidence from the key service's own logs; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the customer's key regional?
clarifications.a: By default yes, one key per region; some customers create linked keys usable in several regions.

clarifications.q: Who triggers rotation?
clarifications.a: The customer, in their key management service. The service must notice and act.

clarifications.q: Does revocation mean the customer deleted the key?
clarifications.a: Usually they remove the service's permission to use it; sometimes they delete it, which cannot be undone.

clarifications.q: Are logical exports covered?
clarifications.a: Customers can export data to their own object storage; say whether and how exports are protected.

clarifications.q: Can the service's support engineers read customer data?
clarifications.a: Not in this design; access to plaintext data is the customer's.

hints: Envelope encryption: the customer's key wraps a small number of data keys; rotation can rewrap those without touching the data files.
A backup taken before a rotation was wrapped by an earlier key version. Write down which key versions every retained backup depends on.
A running member holds unwrapped data keys in memory. Decide how revocation reaches a member that never restarts.
followups: Draw the key hierarchy and show which calls to the key management service happen at member start, at rotation, at backup and at restore.
The customer rotates their key. What changes in the cluster, in its replicas in other regions, and in the backups?
How does the service learn that access has been revoked, and what does it do in each of the first {{revoke_hours}} hours?
A restore is requested of a snapshot taken just before the customer's last two rotations. What must still exist for it to work, and how do you warn a customer before they break it?
How does a customer prove to an auditor that a revocation drill worked, using records the service cannot alter?

rules.ask: Re-encrypting every data file at each rotation costs I/O on {{clusters}} clusters every {{rotation_days}} days. What does rewrapping give up compared with that, and when would you still re-encrypt?
How long may a member keep using a data key it unwrapped before revocation, and how do you enforce that bound?
Stopping members makes the data unreadable, but a member that is down cannot be told to start again later. What is the customer's path back if the revocation was a mistake?
The key service is down for 30 minutes in one region. Is that a revocation? What do members there do, and what do you tell the customer?
A snapshot copied to a second region for disaster recovery: which key wraps it there, and what happens to it when the customer revokes the key in the first region only?

incidents: A customer changes a permission policy on their key by mistake. Running members keep serving, but a member restarted for a routine patch cannot unwrap its keys and stays down; the rolling patch stalls with one member out of three.

A customer rotates their key and deletes the previous key version the same day. The next day a restore of a snapshot taken two days earlier fails, although the snapshot is well inside the {{backup_days}}-day retention.

A customer revokes access during a security incident and expects their data unreadable within {{revoke_hours}} hours. Members in a second region are still serving reads after the {{revoke_hours}}-hour deadline has passed, and a logical export in object storage was never encrypted with their key.
A regional outage of the key management service lasts 35 minutes. An automated check treats every failed call as revocation and starts stopping members across hundreds of healthy clusters.

templates.title: Point-in-time restore from snapshots plus the oplog
templates.subtopic: snapshots, continuous oplog capture, restore verification, retention

sections.scenario: A managed database service offers point-in-time restore: a customer can restore a cluster to any second within the last {{window}}. A typical large cluster holds {{data_tb}} TB and is sharded; its shards together write about {{oplog_gb_hour}} GB of oplog per hour. Snapshots are taken every {{snapshot_hours}} hours and kept under a retention policy the customer chooses (hourly, daily, weekly and monthly copies). The usual request comes in a hurry: someone dropped a collection, or ran an update without a filter, and the customer wants the data as it was one second before, in a new cluster, within {{rto_hours}} hours.
sections.problem: Design the backup and restore system. Cover how snapshots are taken without stopping the cluster and kept consistent across shards; how the oplog of every shard is captured continuously and checked for gaps; how a restore to a chosen second works, from choosing the snapshot to replaying the oplog to a single point across all shards; how a restored cluster is verified before it is handed to the customer; how retention is applied and storage is reclaimed; and how you prove, continuously, that restores work.
sections.constraints: Any second in the last {{window}} is restorable, or the console says plainly which periods are not and why. A restore of a {{data_tb}} TB cluster completes within {{rto_hours}} hours. A multi-document transaction is either fully present in a restored cluster or fully absent. Backups never add more than a few percent to the cluster's own load.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, rates and periods are hypothetical. For this exercise: each shard's oplog is a fixed-size log whose window can be shorter than an hour during heavy writes; oplog entries carry a timestamp of seconds plus an increment, and applying an entry twice leaves the same result; a transaction that spans shards commits at one cluster time on every shard it touched. These are this exercise's rules; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Consistent snapshots per shard plus a cluster-wide restore point defined by cluster time; continuous, idempotent oplog capture per shard with gap detection against the oplog window and alerts that leave headroom; a restore plan that estimates its own duration against {{rto_hours}} hours (bytes to copy, hours of oplog to replay) and keeps it bounded by snapshot frequency or by pre-staged incrementals; transactions kept whole across shards; verification by startup checks, index and collection validation, counts against oplog-derived expectations and regular automated drills; retention as reference-counted deletion with incremental chains understood; non-restorable periods shown honestly; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Restore in place or into a new cluster?
clarifications.a: Both are offered; most urgent restores go into a new cluster so the live one can keep running.

clarifications.q: Does "to a second" include writes in that second?
clarifications.a: Your design must define it and show the definition to the customer; inclusive up to the end of the chosen second is common.

clarifications.q: Are snapshots from storage volumes or from the database?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say what each costs in consistency and speed.

clarifications.q: Can a customer restore one collection only?
clarifications.a: Not in this round; mention how you would add it.

clarifications.q: Who pays for backup storage?
clarifications.a: The customer, per GB per month, so retention changes must reclaim storage promptly.

hints: A restore is a base snapshot plus a replay. Its time is dominated by the bytes copied and the hours of oplog replayed since that snapshot.
Oplog capture is only useful if it never falls behind further than the oplog covers. Measure the gap between capture and the oldest entry still on the shard.
Shards must be restored to the same cluster time, not the same wall-clock second on each shard's clock.
followups: Walk through a restore to 14:03:26 for a sharded cluster: which snapshot, which oplog slices, what is replayed where, and how the shards agree on the stopping point.
What is the worst-case restore time with snapshots every {{snapshot_hours}} hours and {{oplog_gb_hour}} GB of oplog per hour, and what would you change to stay within {{rto_hours}} hours?
How do you detect a gap in captured oplog, and what does the customer see for a period you cannot restore?
How do you verify a restored cluster before handing it over, without comparing it to a source that no longer exists?
A customer shortens retention from a year to a month. What is deleted, in what order, and how do you avoid deleting a snapshot that a restore in progress is using?

rules.ask: An incremental chain is only as good as its oldest link. What happens to restores if one block in the base snapshot is corrupt?
What exactly do you compare a restored cluster against, given that the source cluster has changed since the restore point?
One shard's clock is 3 seconds ahead. Whose second is 14:03:26, and how do you keep a cross-shard transaction whole?
The policy keeps monthly snapshots for a year, but your captured oplog is kept for {{window}}. What can a customer restore to from eleven months ago, exactly?
How many restores a day do you run across the fleet, chosen how, and what fails the drill?

incidents: A customer's bulk import fills one shard's oplog in 40 minutes while oplog capture for that shard is throttled. The oldest needed entry is overwritten before capture reaches it, leaving a 25-minute period that cannot be restored to.

A collection is dropped at 14:03:27 just before the next snapshot was due, {{snapshot_hours}} hours after the last one. Replaying the oplog written since that snapshot, at {{oplog_gb_hour}} GB per hour, takes longer than copying the snapshot itself, and the restore finishes after the {{rto_hours}}-hour promise.

In a restore drill, document counts match, but an order and its inventory reservation, written in one transaction across two shards, appear on one shard only because each shard was stopped at its own wall-clock second.

After a customer shortens retention, their storage bill does not fall for two months: snapshots are still referenced by a long-running restore and by incremental chains whose base was supposed to be deleted.

templates.title: A team metric people have learned to game
templates.subtopic: Goodhart's law, measuring outcomes, changing a target

case: the median time to resolve customer performance escalations keeps falling because tickets are closed as 'waiting on customer' and then reopened as new tickets
the share of slow-query alerts closed within 24 hours keeps rising because alert thresholds were quietly raised on the noisiest clusters
the number of index suggestions customers accepted keeps rising because suggestions were pushed for indexes that were never used afterwards
audience: a dashboard shown to the director every week
the goals two engineers' promotion cases cite

sections.scenario: You lead a team that supports the performance of customers' database clusters. For a year the team has been judged on one headline number. It sits in {{audience}}, and it has improved every quarter. Looking at the underlying records, you find the pattern behind the improvement: {{case}}. Nobody has lied about the number; people did what the target rewarded. Customers' actual experience, judging by repeat escalations and survey comments, has not improved.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you confirm what is happening and how much of the improvement is real, how you raise it with the team without turning it into blame, what you measure instead (and how you stop the new measure being gamed the same way), how you report the change upward when the old number is about to get worse, and what you do about people whose goals were written around the old number. Then tell me about a real time a metric you owned or depended on stopped meaning what it was meant to, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The number is already in {{audience}}. You cannot stop measuring the team's work. Two people on the team set this metric up and are proud of it.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Confirms and quantifies before acting (samples of raw records, a corrected series); owns their part in reporting it; raises it with the team as a system problem, not individual blame, starting with the metric's authors; replaces one gameable number with a balanced set tied to customer outcomes (repeat escalations, time to a confirmed fix, measured latency improvement after a change) plus regular review of raw cases; tells leadership early, with the corrected history and the reason; protects people whose goals relied on the old number; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is anyone breaking a rule?
clarifications.a: No written rule. The behaviour is visible in the records if you look.

clarifications.q: Did you set the metric?
clarifications.a: Your predecessor did; you have reported it for two quarters without questioning it.

clarifications.q: Does the director know?
clarifications.a: Not yet. They have praised the trend in public.

clarifications.q: Do customers see the number?
clarifications.a: No; they see the outcomes.

hints: Quantify first: how much of the improvement survives once the gamed cases are counted honestly?
Name your own part in it. You reported the number too.
Prefer a small set of measures that pull against each other, and keep looking at the raw cases, not only the number.
followups: How do you recompute the last four quarters honestly, and what do you do if the corrected trend is flat?
What do you say to the team, and in what order: the two who built the metric, the whole team, your manager?
Which measures replace it, and how could each of them be gamed?
An engineer's promotion case leans on the old number. What do you do for them?
In your real example, what told you the metric had drifted, and how long did that take?

rules.ask: Every target can be gamed. Which behaviour does your new target reward that you would not want, and how will you notice it?
That signal arrives months late and from few customers. What do you watch week to week?
The people gamed a target that leadership rewarded. Where does accountability sit, including yours?
The director's dashboard shows the corrected number falling next quarter. What do you put beside it so it is not misread?
Which part did you personally decide, and what did it cost you?

templates.title: Disagreeing with your manager's decision, then committing to it
templates.subtopic: upward disagreement, evidence, executing a decision you opposed

decision: to make weekly instead of daily restore drills the default for backups, to save cost; in your view the risk to customers is larger than the saving
to ship the new online schema-migration tool to all customers this quarter instead of a limited preview; in your view it has not been tested on enough real workloads
to deprecate a widely used but costly query-profiling feature in six months; in your view the customers who depend on it have no good replacement yet

sections.scenario: Your manager has decided {{decision}}. You argued against it in the planning meeting. Your manager listened, weighed it against other things they are accountable for, and decided anyway. Your team is responsible for carrying it out over the next {{weeks}} weeks, and two engineers on the team share your view and are asking you what to do.
sections.problem: What do you do now? Cover how you check whether you have made your case as well as it can be made, and whether there is anything new to add; how you decide if this is a case to escalate further or to commit; what you say to the two engineers; how you carry out the decision well, including how you reduce the risk you raised; and what would make you raise it again. Then tell me about a real time you disagreed with a manager's decision and then carried it out, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The decision is within your manager's authority. You still think it is the wrong call. Your team's work on it starts now.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Checks the case was understood (a short written summary, new evidence if any) without relitigating endlessly; distinguishes a judgement call from an issue that must be escalated, and escalates openly if so; commits fully: plans the work well, speaks about the decision honestly but without undermining it; reduces the risk they raised through how the work is done (staging, monitoring, a defined trigger to revisit agreed with the manager); reports early evidence either way; real example with outcome, lessons and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Did your manager explain their reasons?
clarifications.a: Briefly: cost, a commitment made elsewhere, and a view that the risk is manageable.

clarifications.q: Is there an ethical or safety issue?
clarifications.a: Not of the kind that would oblige you to escalate; it is a judgement about risk and value.

clarifications.q: Can the plan be adjusted?
clarifications.a: Within the decision, yes; how it is carried out is largely up to your team.

clarifications.q: Will anyone outside the team know you disagreed?
clarifications.a: Only if you tell them.

hints: Separate "I would decide differently" from "this decision is unsafe or wrong in a way leadership must know". They call for different actions.
Committing does not mean hiding the risk. Measure it, and agree in advance what evidence would reopen the decision.
What you say to the team about a decision you opposed shapes whether they can execute it.
followups: Before you commit, what do you do to be sure your manager has understood your strongest argument?
What do you tell the two engineers, word for word, about your own view?
How do you carry out the decision so that the risk you raised is visible and limited?
Halfway through the {{weeks}} weeks, early data suggests you were right. What do you do, and what if it suggests you were wrong?
In your real example, how did the outcome compare with your prediction, and what did you learn about your own judgement?

rules.ask: What makes this case worth going over your manager's head, and how would you tell them first?
What does committing look like in your calendar next week, concretely?
Which result, by when, would make you raise the decision again, and did you agree that in advance with your manager?
One of the engineers says, "So you think this is a mistake?" in the team meeting. What do you answer?
Which part was your call, and which part was your manager's?

templates.title: Splitting a team that has grown too large to work as one
templates.subtopic: ownership boundaries, on-call, splitting a team

areas: replication, backups and restore, and cluster upgrades
the query planner, indexes and the performance advisor
data import connectors, change streams and the streaming integration
symptom: stand-up takes 40 minutes and nobody listens to most of it
on-call covers so many systems that nobody feels expert in any of them
two senior engineers make most decisions because no one else has the full picture

sections.scenario: Your team has grown to {{size}} engineers over eighteen months. It owns {{areas}}. The signs that it no longer works as one team are everywhere: {{symptom}}, planning takes a week, and new engineers take months to be useful. Your manager asks you to propose how to split it into two or three teams, and to lead the change.
sections.problem: How would you approach it? Cover how you decide the boundaries (by component, by customer journey, by lifecycle or some other cut) and how you test them against real work from the last two quarters; how ownership of code, on-call, roadmaps and customer escalations moves; who leads each new team and how people are placed; how you communicate it; and how you will know in six months whether the split worked. Then tell me about a real time you changed how a team was organised, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: No new headcount. On-call coverage cannot lapse during the change. Some systems are tightly coupled and touched by most changes.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Boundaries chosen from evidence (change coupling, incidents, customer escalations) and tested against past work; single ownership of every system with explicit handling of the unloved component and the single expert; on-call and escalation plans for the transition; fair, transparent placement and lead selection; clear communication, with the reasons; success measures set in advance (dependency count, lead time, on-call load, onboarding time, retention); willingness to adjust; real example with personal contribution and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do the new teams need managers?
clarifications.a: One more manager can be hired or promoted; for the rest, decide with your manager.

clarifications.q: Can engineers choose their team?
clarifications.a: Preferences can be asked for; the final placement is yours and your manager's.

clarifications.q: Are there systems nobody wants to own?
clarifications.a: Yes, an older component that pages often and has one expert.

clarifications.q: How soon?
clarifications.a: Within a quarter, without dropping committed work.

hints: Draw boundaries where changes rarely need two teams. Look at which code changed together and which incidents crossed areas.
Every system needs exactly one owner after the split, including the unloved one.
Plan on-call and customer escalations explicitly; they are where splits fail first.
followups: Using the last two quarters' work, how do you test whether your boundary would have produced fewer cross-team dependencies?
Which team owns the older component that pages often, and what do you do about its single expert?
How do you split on-call without leaving any system thinly covered during the transition?
Two engineers both want to lead the same new team. How do you decide, and what do you do for the one not chosen?
Six months on, what numbers and conversations tell you whether the split worked, and what would make you change it again?

rules.ask: Which part of your system's architecture would you want to change to fit the new teams, and is that worth doing?
During the transition, who is paged for a system whose owner has just changed, and who do they call when they are stuck?
Most engineers ask for the same new team. What do you do with that information?
A shared component is touched by every team. Who decides its roadmap, and how do the others get changes made?
Which decision did you personally make, and who disagreed with it?

templates.title: Recovering trust after the team missed a commitment it made publicly
templates.subtopic: missed public commitment, communication, rebuilding credibility

commitment: general availability of a new backup feature on a date announced at a user conference
a public roadmap date for a connector several large customers planned around
a published fix date for a known issue that made some scheduled backups skip silently
cause: testing found the change could lose data in a rare failover case
a dependency team's work slipped and nobody escalated
the estimate was made before the design was understood

sections.scenario: Your team owned {{commitment}}. The date has been missed, {{slip}}. The cause is that {{cause}}. Customers who planned around the date are frustrated; account teams who repeated the date to customers feel let down; and your own leadership is asking how this happened and whether the next date can be believed.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover the first days (what you communicate, to whom, and with what honesty about the cause and the new date), how you decide when to give a new date and how confident it must be, how you support the customers who planned around the old one, what you change in how your team makes and tracks commitments, and how you rebuild trust over the following months. Then tell me about a real time your team missed a commitment others relied on, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Shipping something unsafe to hit a date is not an option. You cannot promise a date you do not believe. Account teams need something to tell customers this week.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Owns the miss, including the unraised warning signs; communicates quickly and honestly to account teams and leadership, with the cause, what customers can do now, and when the next update comes; gives a new date only as a range with its dependencies, at a confidence that is stated; supports affected customers directly, and weighs a preview on safety evidence; changes how the team raises date risks (explicit confidence, early escalation triggers, dependency tracking); rebuilds trust through visible, kept smaller commitments; real example with personal contribution and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Did you know the date was at risk before it was missed?
clarifications.a: There were warning signs a month earlier; they were discussed but not raised outside the team.

clarifications.q: Are customers harmed, or only inconvenienced?
clarifications.a: Some changed their own plans and budgets around the date.

clarifications.q: Can part of it ship?
clarifications.a: Possibly a limited preview for a few customers; you decide whether that helps or adds risk.

clarifications.q: Who announced the date publicly?
clarifications.a: Product leadership, based on your team's estimate.

hints: Start with the facts and your part in them, including the month when the risk was known and not raised.
A new date is only useful if it is believed; give a range with what it depends on, and update it on a known schedule.
Trust comes back from a run of small commitments kept, not from one large promise.
followups: What exactly do you send account teams this week, and what do you not say?
How do you build the new estimate, and how confident must you be before it is public?
What changes in how your team raises a risk to a date, so the month of warning signs does not happen again?
A large customer asks for an early preview to stay on their own plan. What do you weigh?
In your real example, how long did it take for others to trust your dates again, and what made the difference?

rules.ask: An apology without a believable plan can make things worse. What comes with yours?
Padding every estimate will make the next date safe and the roadmap slow. How do you keep estimates honest instead?
The preview has the bug that caused the slip in a rarer form. Who decides whether it ships, and on what evidence?
Who receives those updates, and what makes them trust the next one more than the last?
Which part of the miss was yours personally, and what did you change in your own practice?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a distributed document database
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, documents, replication and sharding

angle: the data model and its access patterns
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: records whose shape differs by customer and changes every month
writes that must survive the loss of any one region
a dataset that outgrows one machine and must be split by a key chosen now
reads from replicas that must never show a customer an older state than they have already seen

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if its data, at {{scale}}, lived in a distributed document database with replica sets and sharding, and its users required {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes if the data were stored as documents in a replicated, sharded database with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The document-database setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to entities, keys, access patterns and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible document-database analysis that starts from access patterns, names embedding and referencing choices and unbounded growth, and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example versioned documents with a schema-version field and validation rules, majority writes with members placed so no region holds a majority, a shard key with high cardinality and even write spread chosen from real queries, causally consistent sessions or primary reads where order matters); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a database project?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that stored, moved or computed data others depended on; the document-database part is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to entities, keys, access patterns, consistency, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the document-database question, start from the access patterns: which data is read together, which grows without bound, and which key spreads the writes.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which of your entities would you embed in one document and which would you reference, and why?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite, and what would it cost?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Why that over the obvious alternative, and what did it cost you?
One of those embedded arrays grows without limit for your largest customer. What happens to the document and to every write that touches it?
One customer is a hundred times larger than the rest. Where does their data live under your key, and what happens to that shard?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
